items.questionAndWhy: Is “social behavior” genetically one stable trait, or do its associations change depending on which behavior is measured, who reports it, and when in development it is observed? The distinction matters because broad trait scores can hide meaningful context dependence.
items.whatTheyDid: de Hoyos and colleagues meta-analyzed 491,246 repeated measures from 73,321 people across 25 cohorts, spanning ages 2–29. Their genome-wide meta-regression modeled variation across low prosocial behavior versus peer/social difficulties, parent/teacher/self reports, and developmental stage, then tested context-matched polygenic scores in independent cohorts.
items.whatTheyFound: They identified six associated loci, including CADM2, but common variants explained only a small share of variance: SNP-based heritability estimates were roughly 2–7%. Genetic associations varied systematically by social domain, reporter, and age, and context-matched polygenic scores predicted better than mismatched ones, although incremental predictive power remained small (up to about 1.3%). The discovery sample was predominantly European ancestry, limiting generalization.
items.whatItMeans: Even the genetic architecture of a broad construct such as social behavior can depend on context and measurement. For PSYWERX, the strongest lesson is not a genetic one: combining reporter, age, and behavior type into one undifferentiated score can erase structure that matters. Polygenic scores here are weak population-level predictors, not deterministic individual profiles.
items.streamTitle: Social behavior’s genetic signals changed with age, reporter, and social context
items.streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study analyzed nearly 500,000 repeated social-behavior measures from 73,321 people and found that genetic associations varied with age, whether the outcome was low prosocial behavior or peer difficulties, and whether parents, teachers, or participants reported it. Common variants explained only about 2–7% of variance, and context-matched polygenic scores performed better but still added little predictive power. The study’s main lesson is measurement: “social behavior” is not one context-free trait. The discovery sample was predominantly European ancestry, which also limits generalization.
items.attribution: de Hoyos et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.questionAndWhy: When people see a group opinion that differs from their own, is conformity just short-term compliance, or can it persist—and does persistence depend on whether the norm pushes behavior in a pro- or anti-climate direction?
items.whatTheyDid: Yeon and colleagues tested 47 Korean university students across 113 pro-climate behaviors. Participants first reported their own intentions, then saw experimentally generated peer norms that were congruent, moderately different, or highly different and either more pro-climate or less pro-climate. They rated their intentions again immediately and seven days later while EEG captured responses during the initial session.
items.whatTheyFound: Immediate conformity increased as the gap from the presented norm grew, regardless of whether the norm was pro- or anti-climate. Seven days later, conformity remained elevated for pro-climate norms but was not sustained for anti-climate norms. Stronger personal pro-climate norms predicted less conformity, and EEG responses also differed by norm direction. The sample was small, the peer opinions were synthetic, and the outcome was stated intention rather than observed behavior.
items.whatItMeans: Social influence can look symmetric in the moment and asymmetric over time. That makes persistence a separate outcome from immediate movement and suggests that the content of a norm can matter for whether compliance becomes internalized. The study is best treated as a mechanism probe, not evidence that one-week opinion shifts will translate into real-world climate behavior.
items.streamTitle: Social norms shifted climate intentions immediately in both directions, but only pro-climate shifts persisted
items.streamSummary: A small EEG experiment exposed 47 Korean university students to experimentally generated peer norms about 113 pro-climate behaviors. Participants moved their stated intentions toward both pro- and anti-climate group opinions immediately, especially when the group differed more from them. One week later, however, the shift remained for pro-climate norms but not anti-climate norms. Stronger personal norms reduced conformity. The study suggests short-term compliance and longer-term internalization may differ, but the sample was small, the peer opinions were synthetic, and the outcome was behavioral intention rather than observed behavior.

items.questionAndWhy: How might routine generative-AI use relate to employees taking initiative at work? The authors tested whether AI use is associated with a more absorbing “flow” state and with feeling less objectified at work, rather than assuming productivity effects operate through one pathway.
items.whatTheyDid: Xu and colleagues ran a three-wave time-lagged survey with 380 full-time knowledge workers. They measured generative-AI use, flow experience, workplace objectification, proactive behavior, and digital literacy, then estimated a dual-pathway mediation model.
items.whatTheyFound: More generative-AI use was associated with more self-reported proactive behavior, partly through greater flow and lower workplace objectification. Digital literacy strengthened the association between AI use and lower objectification, but did not significantly strengthen the AI-to-flow relationship. Because the study is observational and largely self-reported, the pathways are associations rather than demonstrated causal effects of AI use.
items.whatItMeans: Human-AI effects can plausibly run through different psychological experiences at the same time. For workplace evaluation, measuring only output can miss whether AI changes engagement, agency, or how people feel treated. The study also illustrates why time-lagged surveys should not be described as causal simply because variables were measured at different waves.
items.streamTitle: Generative-AI use was linked to more proactive work behavior through two different workplace experiences
items.streamSummary: A three-wave survey of 380 full-time knowledge workers found that heavier generative-AI use was associated with more self-reported proactive behavior. Two statistical pathways helped explain the relationship: greater flow and lower workplace objectification. Digital literacy strengthened the link between AI use and lower objectification, but did not significantly strengthen the flow pathway. The result is useful for thinking about human-AI work beyond raw productivity, but the study is observational and mostly self-reported. It therefore identifies plausible mechanisms and moderators rather than proving that increasing AI use will cause employees to become more proactive.

items.questionAndWhy: When online diets become polarized, repetitive, or filled with problematic content, how much is caused by recommendation algorithms and how much comes from what users actively choose? The distinction matters because interventions will fail if they target the wrong causal mechanism.
items.whatTheyDid: Hosseinmardi, Dutta, Rothschild, Watts and colleagues reviewed research on algorithmic recommendation and users’ self-selection across digital platforms. They organize platform behavior as a feedback system in which algorithms shape exposure while users’ preferences, choices, and engagement simultaneously shape what algorithms serve next.
items.whatTheyFound: The review concludes that evidence directly linking algorithmic curation to many problematic societal outcomes remains inconclusive, while user preference and self-selection are often underweighted in public and research explanations. The authors call for more large-scale experiments and data that can separate the two mechanisms. This is a review and research agenda, not a new causal estimate of platform effects.
items.whatItMeans: “The algorithm did it” and “users chose it” are not competing complete explanations; they can form a reinforcing loop. For influence and platform research, exposure, selection, engagement, and subsequent recommendation should be modeled as separate steps so interventions can target the part of the loop that actually produces the outcome.
items.streamTitle: A major platform review says recommender effects cannot be separated from user self-selection
items.streamSummary: A new Nature Computational Science review argues that research and public debate often attribute harmful online outcomes too quickly to recommendation algorithms while underestimating users’ own preferences and self-selection. Reviewing both literatures, the authors find that evidence tying algorithmic curation to many problematic outcomes remains inconclusive and call for large-scale experiments that separate algorithmic exposure from what people actively choose. The key implication is a feedback-loop model: users shape what systems learn, systems shape what users see, and users respond again. The paper is a synthesis and research agenda rather than a new causal estimate.
items.attribution: Hosseinmardi et al. — Nature Computational Science

items.questionAndWhy: How can organizations quantify privacy risk inside a trained machine-learning model instead of treating privacy as a checklist? The study focuses on whether attack-based testing can create a practical risk score relevant to privacy-by-design decisions.
items.whatTheyDid: Han combined model-inversion, membership-inference, and attribute-inference attacks into a 0–100 privacy-risk methodology. The framework was tested across deep neural networks, decision trees, support-vector machines, and other model families using five standard benchmark datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: The method reported an average privacy-risk detection accuracy of 89.3% across its experiments. Deep neural networks produced higher mean risk scores in the tested setups (74.1) than ensemble approaches (51.6). These are benchmark results produced by a particular attack suite and scoring method; they do not constitute a legal determination of GDPR compliance or prove the same ranking will hold in a specific deployed system.
items.whatItMeans: Privacy can be evaluated empirically by trying to extract information from the model, not only by documenting governance controls. For PSYWERX-style AI TEVV, the useful pattern is to keep utility, privacy attack success, and organizational/legal compliance as separate dimensions rather than inferring one from another.
items.streamTitle: A new privacy-risk framework scores machine-learning models by how well common attacks can extract sensitive information
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study proposes a 0–100 privacy-risk score built from three attack families: model inversion, membership inference, and attribute inference. Tested across multiple model architectures and five benchmark datasets, the method reported 89.3% average detection accuracy; deep neural networks had higher mean risk scores than ensemble approaches in the tested setups. The framework offers a practical way to make privacy testing more empirical, but its benchmark scores are not a legal judgment of GDPR compliance and may not transfer directly to a specific production environment. Utility, attack vulnerability, and governance still need separate assessment.

items.questionAndWhy: Would the U.S.–China AI discussions produce a concrete risk-reduction proposal or remain a broad agenda item? A notification channel could matter if serious AI incidents need to be clarified before they are misread as deliberate hostile action.
items.whatTheyDid: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng concluded roughly eight hours of talks in New York on September 20. The U.S. side proposed an AI-safety notification mechanism and a bilateral dialogue focused on national security, transparency, and significant AI incidents for Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to consider at their upcoming summit.
items.whatTheyFound: The proposal is a material development from the previous day’s agenda-level reporting, but it is not yet an agreement. China’s public response was vague, no formal AI forum had been established, and high-end AI-chip export controls were not part of these talks. The reporting therefore establishes a proposed mechanism, not shared thresholds, verification rules, or implementation.
items.whatItMeans: Incident notification is a narrower and potentially more testable guardrail than a generic commitment to “AI safety.” If adopted, its value would depend on what triggers notification, how quickly information is exchanged, which incidents are covered, and whether each side trusts the information enough to prevent escalation.
items.streamTitle: U.S.–China AI talks moved from a general agenda to a proposed incident-notification mechanism
items.streamSummary: U.S. and Chinese officials concluded New York talks with a more concrete AI proposal than the agenda reported the day before. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the U.S. proposed a bilateral mechanism for notifying each other about significant AI incidents, alongside a dialogue focused on national security and transparency for Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to consider. China’s public response remained vague, and no formal mechanism has been agreed. The development is therefore a proposed crisis-management tool, not an implemented safeguard. Its usefulness would depend on notification thresholds, speed, scope, verification, and mutual trust.

items.questionAndWhy: What changed after months of investigation and the August removal of two of China’s most senior military officers from the Central Military Commission? Formal party and military expulsion clarifies their status, while leaving the operational consequences much harder to infer.
items.whatTheyDid: On September 21, Chinese authorities announced the disciplinary findings against Zhang Youxia, formerly a Central Military Commission vice-chairman and Politburo member, and Liu Zhenli, formerly a CMC member and Joint Staff Department chief. The Communist Party leadership approved their expulsion from the party and military; state reporting alleged serious political, organizational, integrity, and corruption violations.
items.whatTheyFound: The expulsions formalize a leadership rupture that began with investigations in January and removal from the state CMC in August. Reuters notes that Zhang was one of the PLA’s few senior officers with combat experience and had been a close Xi Jinping ally. The underlying misconduct allegations come from China’s disciplinary authorities and have not been independently adjudicated in an open process.
items.whatItMeans: The observable fact is a large change in senior command personnel; the downstream military effect remains an analytical question. Leadership turnover can affect continuity, expertise, promotion incentives, and loyalty signaling, but it should not automatically be translated into a quantified loss of readiness or combat effectiveness without evidence.
items.streamTitle: China formally expelled two top generals, turning a months-long investigation into a major command-level personnel change
items.streamSummary: Chinese authorities announced the formal expulsion of former Central Military Commission vice-chairman Zhang Youxia and former Joint Staff chief Liu Zhenli from the Communist Party and military on September 21. The move follows investigations opened in January and their removal from the state CMC in August. State reporting alleges extensive disciplinary, loyalty, and corruption violations; those allegations come from China’s internal disciplinary process. The strategic significance is clear at the personnel level, but the operational effect is not: command turnover may affect continuity, expertise, and incentives, yet it does not by itself demonstrate reduced PLA readiness.

items.questionAndWhy: How can commanders understand cyber conditions as mission risk rather than as a stream of technical alerts? The practitioner proposal asks whether defensive cyber, offensive cyber, and AI-enabled analysis can be fused into one operational picture tied to ships, logistics, command nodes, and maneuver.
items.whatTheyDid: Navy Reserve Lt. Nathaniel Taylor proposes an “aitaeon,” an autonomous adaptive multi-domain cyber common operational picture. The concept would fuse defensive and offensive cyber data, global sensing, digital emulation, and AI-supported detection, target development, course-of-action generation, and risk visualization into a commander-centric view.
items.whatTheyFound: This is a professional concept, not an operational trial. The article argues that the approach could translate cyber conditions into mission-relevant risk and synchronize cyber effects with maneuver and fires, while also warning that adversary data manipulation, degraded connectivity, false positives, overreliance on AI, and unintended escalation could make the system brittle without red-teaming and graceful degradation.
items.whatItMeans: The strongest idea is architectural: technical cyber indicators become more useful when explicitly mapped to operational consequences and decisions. For evaluation, the right questions are whether the picture improves decisions, survives manipulated or missing data, keeps uncertainty visible, and performs better than simpler workflows—not whether it looks comprehensive.
items.streamTitle: A Navy practitioner proposal turns cyber data into a mission-focused AI common operational picture
items.streamSummary: A September U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings article proposes an AI-enabled cyber common operational picture that fuses defensive cyber, offensive cyber, sensing, digital emulation, and human-AI decision support into a mission-focused view for naval commanders. The author argues this could translate technical cyber conditions into risks to strike groups, logistics routes, and command nodes. It is a concept, not a validated operational system, and the article itself warns about data manipulation, degraded connectivity, false positives, overreliance on AI, and escalation. The useful test is therefore decision improvement under contested conditions, not dashboard completeness.
items.attribution: Lt. Nathaniel Taylor, U.S. Navy Reserve — Proceedings

items.questionAndWhy: Does air pollution reduce productivity even in high-skilled knowledge work, not only in physically demanding jobs? If so, environmental conditions become part of the performance context for cognitive work.
items.whatTheyDid: Dong, Qiao, and Zhou combined Chinese air-quality measurements with longitudinal bibliographic data on scholars and used an instrumental-variable design to estimate the effect of annual PM2.5 exposure on publication output. They also examined work hours, hospital visits, collaboration, nonlinear effects, and differences across scholar groups.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors estimate that a 1 microgram-per-cubic-meter increase in annual PM2.5 is associated, under their instrumental-variable assumptions, with a 0.23% decline in publications. Effects were larger in heavily polluted years and among younger and highly productive scholars. Higher pollution was also linked to fewer working hours, more hospital visits, and weaker collaboration. The causal interpretation depends on the validity of the instrument and other design assumptions.
items.whatItMeans: Environmental context can affect high-skill output through health, available work time, and collaboration—not just through obvious physical impairment. For behavioral or workforce models, “capability” should not be treated as entirely internal to the person. The study is strong quasi-experimental evidence, but its exact effect size should not be assumed to transport outside the studied Chinese academic context.
items.streamTitle: An instrumental-variable study estimates that PM2.5 pollution reduces high-skilled research output
items.streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study combined Chinese air-quality data with scholars’ publication records and used an instrumental-variable design to estimate how PM2.5 affects knowledge-work productivity. The authors estimate that each 1 μg/m³ increase in annual PM2.5 reduced publication output by about 0.23%, with larger effects in heavily polluted years and among younger and highly productive scholars. Higher pollution was also associated with fewer working hours, more hospital visits, and weaker collaboration. The design is stronger than a simple correlation, but the causal estimate still depends on instrument validity and should not be assumed to generalize unchanged beyond Chinese academia.
items.attribution: Dong, Qiao & Zhou — Nature Human Behaviour

items.questionAndWhy: If a field reports that 50% of studies replicate, is that good, bad, or exactly what should be expected? The answer requires a benchmark, but replication debates often treat the observed percentage itself as a quality score.
items.whatTheyDid: Mark Rubin’s Nature Human Behaviour Comment evaluates two possible benchmarks: an “optimal” replication rate and an “expected” replication rate. He examines the limitations of using either as a universal target and argues that researchers need better education about what replication percentages can and cannot tell them.
items.whatTheyFound: The central conclusion is conceptual: there is no clear universal target that makes an observed replication rate self-interpreting. A field’s rate depends on the mix of true effects, statistical power, designs, analytic choices, and the way replication attempts are sampled and defined. This is an argument about interpretation, not a new empirical replication project.
items.whatItMeans: Replication rate should not become another context-free dashboard metric. For evidence governance, the useful question is why a particular result failed or succeeded to replicate and what the expected rate should be under the study portfolio—not whether the field clears an arbitrary percentage threshold.
items.streamTitle: A replication rate has no obvious meaning without a defensible target rate
items.streamSummary: A new Nature Human Behaviour Comment asks a deceptively simple question: if 50% of studies replicate, what should that number be compared with? Mark Rubin evaluates “optimal” and “expected” target replication rates and argues that neither provides a simple universal benchmark. Replication percentages depend on power, the mix of true and null effects, study designs, analytic choices, and how replications are selected and defined. The piece is conceptual rather than a new replication experiment. Its practical lesson is that replication rate should not be treated as a standalone quality score without a defensible model of what rate should have been expected.
